evals.prompt: We launched 10 `t3.medium` instances in ap-south-1 for a video-processing worker service that runs at a steady 80% CPU utilization 24/7. We didn't change any credit settings at launch, and our monthly EC2 bill is suddenly way higher than the base `t3.medium` hourly rate! Why did this happen, what happens to CPU credits if we stop `t3`/`t4g` vs `t2` instances, and how should we fix our fleet?
evals.expected_output: Activates the aws-compute skill, explains that `t3`, `t3a`, and `t4g` instances default to `unlimited` mode (unlike `t2` which defaults to `standard`), where running sustained 80% CPU above the 20% baseline depletes accrued CPU credits and silently bills **surplus CPU credits** (`CPUSurplusCreditsCharged`), explains credit persistence on stop (`t2` Standard loses all accrued credits on stop, whereas `t3`/`t3a`/`t4g` preserve their credit balance for 7 days after stop), and recommends either migrating steady high-CPU workloads to fixed-performance compute/general-purpose instances (`c7g`/`c8g`/`m7g`/`m8g`) or switching credit specification to `standard` (`modify-instance-credit-specification`).
expectations: Activates the aws-compute skill and explains that `t3`/`t3a`/`t4g` instances default to `unlimited` credit mode, causing sustained 80% CPU utilization above the 20% baseline to bill surplus CPU credits (`CPUSurplusCreditsCharged`)
Explains CPU credit behavior on instance stop: `t2` Standard resets accrued credits to zero on stop, whereas `t3`, `t3a`, and `t4g` retain their CPU credit balance for 7 days after stopping
Recommends migrating steady high-CPU workloads to fixed-performance instance families (`c7g`/`m7g`) or setting `CpuCredits=standard` via `modify-instance-credit-specification`

evals.prompt: We have two broken Auto Scaling groups behind Application Load Balancers in ap-south-1: (1) On `orders-asg`, our app crashed and returns HTTP 500 on `/health`, the ALB Target Group marks the instances `unhealthy`, but the ASG never terminates or replaces them; (2) On `reporting-asg`, we enabled `--health-check-type ELB` with `--health-check-grace-period 10`, and our Spring Boot app takes 120 seconds to boot — now the ASG kills and replaces every new instance in an endless loop. Diagnose and fix both ASGs.
evals.expected_output: Activates the aws-compute skill and diagnoses both ASG health check pitfalls: (1) ASGs default to `EC2` status checks only and ignore ALB target group health unless `--health-check-type ELB` is explicitly configured; (2) CLI/SDK defaults `--health-check-grace-period` to `0` (here set to `10`s), which is shorter than the 120-second application boot time, causing the ASG to mark booting instances unhealthy via ELB checks and terminate them repeatedly — fixed by raising `--health-check-grace-period` (e.g., `300` seconds) and setting `DefaultInstanceWarmup`.
expectations: Activates the aws-compute skill and explains that ASGs only use `EC2` status checks by default and ignore load balancer target group health until `--health-check-type ELB` is enabled

Explains that `reporting-asg` is in a replacement flap loop because `--health-check-grace-period 10` expires before the 120-second Spring Boot startup completes (noting the CLI/SDK default is `0`s while the console default is `300`s)

Provides the `update-auto-scaling-group` fix setting `--health-check-type ELB` and `--health-check-grace-period 300` (along with `DefaultInstanceWarmup` and verifying `instance` target type on `attach-traffic-sources`)

evals.prompt: We updated our Launch Template with a new AMI and ran `aws autoscaling start-instance-refresh --auto-scaling-group-name prod-api-asg`, where `prod-api-asg` references `Version=$Default` and has `SkipMatching: true`. First, the instance refresh completed immediately after replacing 0 instances! Second, when we tried to enable `AutoRollback: true`, AWS rejected the request. Why did both happen and how do we configure zero-downtime rolling replacements with automatic rollback?
evals.expected_output: Activates the aws-compute skill, explains that with `SkipMatching` enabled, Instance Refresh skips instances that already match the target configuration — when the ASG points at `$Default` (without updating `$Default` to the new version) or an unchanged SSM parameter AMI, 0 instances are replaced; then explains that **AutoRollback is unsupported when the Launch Template version is `$Latest` or `$Default` or when the AMI is an SSM parameter**, requiring pinning an explicit numeric Launch Template version (e.g., `Version='4'`) and configuring `MinHealthyPercentage: 100` with `MaxHealthyPercentage: 120`–`200` (spread <= 100) and staged `Checkpoints`.
expectations: Activates the aws-compute skill and explains why `SkipMatching` replaced 0 instances when the ASG's `$Default` Launch Template version was not updated or pointed to an unchanged configuration
Explains that `AutoRollback` is unsupported when the Launch Template uses `$Latest` or `$Default` (or an SSM parameter AMI) and requires pinning an explicit numeric Launch Template version

Shows configuring `start-instance-refresh` with `MinHealthyPercentage: 100` and `MaxHealthyPercentage` between `100` and `200` (so replacement instances launch before old ones terminate) plus staged `Checkpoints`

evals.prompt: New EC2 instances in our Auto Scaling group in ap-south-1 get stuck in `Pending:Wait` for exactly 1 hour and are then terminated before ever joining the ALB. How do ASG launch lifecycle hooks work, why are instances killed after 1 hour, and how should we harden the IAM notification role and SNS/SQS target used by the lifecycle hook?
evals.expected_output: Activates the aws-compute skill, explains that a launch lifecycle hook pauses instances in `Pending:Wait` with a default heartbeat timeout of **3600 seconds (1 hour)** and a default `DefaultResult` of **`ABANDON`**, which terminates the instance if `complete-lifecycle-action --lifecycle-action-result CONTINUE` (or `record-lifecycle-action-heartbeat`) is never called; and explains hardening the notification pipeline by adding `aws:SourceArn` (the ASG ARN) and `aws:SourceAccount` conditions to the **IAM service role's trust policy** (`autoscaling.amazonaws.com`) to prevent confused-deputy attacks, enabling SSE-KMS on the SNS topic/SQS queue, and restricting topic/queue access policies.
expectations: Activates the aws-compute skill and explains that lifecycle hooks default to a `3600`s (1-hour) heartbeat timeout and `DefaultResult=ABANDON`, causing uncompleted launch hooks to terminate the instance from `Pending:Wait`

Shows completing or extending the hook via `complete-lifecycle-action --lifecycle-action-result CONTINUE` / `record-lifecycle-action-heartbeat` (or setting `DefaultResult=CONTINUE` for non-blocking hooks)

Specifies adding `aws:SourceArn` and `aws:SourceAccount` conditions to the `autoscaling.amazonaws.com` IAM notification role trust policy (not the SNS/SQS policy) and enabling SSE-KMS on the SNS topic or SQS queue

evals.prompt: We hardened our EC2 Launch Template in ap-south-1 by setting `MetadataOptions: {HttpTokens: "required", HttpPutResponseHopLimit: 1}` and passing our database password inside the `UserData` bash script (`export DB_PASS='SuperSecret123'`). Now: (1) our host-level SSM agent works fine, but Docker containers running on the EC2 instance time out or get `401 Unauthorized` when fetching IAM role credentials from `169.254.169.254`, and (2) our security auditor flagged `UserData` as a critical credential leak. Explain both issues and show the corrected Launch Template.
evals.expected_output: Activates the aws-compute skill, explains that `HttpPutResponseHopLimit=1` sets the IP packet TTL on the IMDSv2 `PUT /latest/api/token` response to `1`, so the extra network hop across the Docker bridge causes the token response to be dropped (requiring `HttpPutResponseHopLimit=2` for bridge-networked containers on EC2 while keeping `HttpTokens="required"`); notes that account-level `modify-instance-metadata-defaults` only affects new launches; and explains all 4 places `UserData` exposes secrets (stored unencrypted, readable by any local process via `http://169.254.169.254/latest/user-data`, echoed to `/var/log/cloud-init-output.log`, and recorded in the `RunInstances` CloudTrail event `requestParameters`), recommending fetching secrets at boot from Secrets Manager or SSM Parameter Store `SecureString`.
expectations: Activates the aws-compute skill and explains that `HttpPutResponseHopLimit=1` drops the IMDSv2 session token `PUT` response across the container bridge hop, requiring `HttpPutResponseHopLimit=2` with `HttpTokens=required` for containerized workloads on EC2
Notes that `modify-instance-metadata-defaults` applies only to new instance launches and existing instances require `modify-instance-metadata-options`

Explains why secrets must never be placed in `UserData` (unencrypted storage, readable via IMDS `/latest/user-data`, logged in `/var/log/cloud-init-output.log`, and visible in CloudTrail `RunInstances` `requestParameters`) and replaces it with runtime retrieval from Secrets Manager or SSM Parameter Store

evals.prompt: We have EC2 instances in isolated private subnets (no NAT Gateway, no Internet Gateway) in ap-south-1. Some instances don't show up in Systems Manager Fleet Manager at all, others fail `aws ssm start-session` with `TargetNotConnected`, and our compliance team wants Session Manager logs encrypted in CloudWatch Logs (`cloudWatchEncryptionEnabled=true`). Explain the two ways an instance registers as a managed node (and which takes precedence), the exact VPC endpoints required in a no-NAT subnet, and the gotcha with `cloudWatchEncryptionEnabled=true`.
evals.expected_output: Activates the aws-compute skill, explains the two registration methods: (1) an attached IAM Instance Profile with `AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore`, or (2) account/Region **Default Host Management Configuration (DHMC)** (`AWSSystemsManagerDefaultEC2InstanceManagementRole` with `AmazonSSMManagedEC2InstanceDefaultPolicy`, requiring IMDSv2 — noting that if an instance profile is attached, SSM Agent uses it before DHMC unless `ssm:UpdateInstanceInformation` is removed); lists the required VPC endpoints (`com.amazonaws.ap-south-1.ssm`, `com.amazonaws.ap-south-1.ssmmessages`, free Gateway endpoint `com.amazonaws.ap-south-1.s3` for Patch Manager/Run Command, and `com.amazonaws.ap-south-1.kms` when session `kmsKeyId` is set, noting `ec2messages` is legacy); and explains that `cloudWatchEncryptionEnabled=true` / `s3EncryptionEnabled=true` do NOT encrypt the destination themselves — they are enforcement gates that fail session logging unless the CloudWatch Log Group (`aws logs associate-kms-key`) or S3 bucket is already KMS-encrypted.
expectations: Activates the aws-compute skill and compares the two ways an EC2 instance becomes an SSM managed node (`AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore` instance profile vs Default Host Management Configuration `DHMC`), noting that an attached instance profile takes precedence over DHMC

Lists the required VPC endpoints for isolated no-NAT subnets: `ssm` and `ssmmessages` Interface Endpoints (noting `ec2messages` is legacy), the free `s3` Gateway Endpoint for Patch Manager/artifacts, and the `kms` Interface Endpoint when session encryption (`kmsKeyId`) is enabled

Explains that `cloudWatchEncryptionEnabled=true` and `s3EncryptionEnabled=true` are enforcement gates that do not enable encryption themselves and refuse to stream session logs unless the CloudWatch Log Group (`associate-kms-key`) or S3 bucket is pre-encrypted with KMS

evals.prompt: Our security team found a vulnerable library in last month's production AMI (`ami-0123456789abcdef0`) in ap-south-1. A junior engineer ran `aws ec2 enable-image-deprecation` thinking that would stop Auto Scaling groups from launching new instances from it. Did that actually block launches? Compare `deprecate`, `disable`, and `deregister` (including reversibility and sharing side effects), and also explain why another AWS account gets a KMS error when trying to launch our encrypted golden AMI even after we granted them launch permission.
evals.expected_output: Activates the aws-compute skill, explains that `enable-image-deprecation` only hides the AMI from `describe-images` / console listings for other accounts after the deprecation date — **anyone with the AMI ID (including ASGs and Launch Templates) can still launch instances from a deprecated AMI**; compares it against `disable-image` (sets state to `disabled`, **blocks all new launches**, and revokes launch permissions/sharing; reversible via `enable-image`, though cross-account launch permissions must be re-granted via `modify-image-attribute`) and `deregister-image` (permanently deletes the AMI unless a Recycle Bin retention rule was configured beforehand); and explains that AMIs encrypted with the **default AWS-managed EBS key (`aws/ebs`) cannot be shared across accounts**, requiring re-encrypting snapshots with a **customer-managed KMS key** and granting the target account `kms:DescribeKey`, `kms:Decrypt`, `kms:CreateGrant`, `kms:ReEncrypt*`, and `kms:GenerateDataKey*`.
expectations: Activates the aws-compute skill and explains that `enable-image-deprecation` only hides the AMI from listings and does NOT stop Auto Scaling groups or users with the AMI ID from launching it

Contrasts `disable-image` (immediately blocks new launches and revokes sharing, reversible via `enable-image` + re-granting `modify-image-attribute` launch permissions) with `deregister-image` (permanent removal unless an AWS Recycle Bin retention rule was pre-configured)

Explains that snapshots encrypted with the default AWS-managed key (`aws/ebs`) cannot be shared cross-account, requiring re-encryption under a customer-managed KMS key and granting `kms:DescribeKey`, `kms:Decrypt`, `kms:CreateGrant`, `kms:ReEncrypt*`, and `kms:GenerateDataKey*` to the target account

evals.prompt: Walk our on-call SREs through the exact diagnostic matrix for three sets of look-alike EC2 errors in ap-south-1: (1) SSH failing with `Connection timed out` vs `Connection refused` vs `Permission denied (publickey)`, (2) `StatusCheckFailed_System` vs `StatusCheckFailed_Instance` vs attached EBS impairment, and (3) `InsufficientInstanceCapacity` vs `InstanceLimitExceeded` (`VcpuLimitExceeded`).
evals.expected_output: Activates the aws-compute skill and decodes all three matrices: (1) **SSH**: `Connection timed out` = network layer (SG, NACL, missing IGW route, or public IP changed after stop/start without an Elastic IP), `Connection refused` = host reachable but `sshd` down or still booting, `Permission denied (publickey)` = auth layer (wrong AMI username like `ec2-user` vs `ubuntu` vs `admin`, key perms not `chmod 400`, or EC2 Instance Connect temporary key expired after **60 seconds**); (2) **Status Checks**: `StatusCheckFailed_System` = AWS host hardware failure fixed by **stop/start** (not reboot, which stays on the same physical host), `StatusCheckFailed_Instance` = guest OS/network issue fixed by reboot/serial console, and attached EBS impairment requires the opt-in ASG EBS health check on Nitro instances for automatic replacement; and (3) **Capacity vs Quota**: `InsufficientInstanceCapacity` = AWS lacks spare capacity in that AZ (NOT a quota — try another AZ, instance type, or smaller batch; in a Cluster placement group, stop/start all members), whereas `InstanceLimitExceeded` / `VcpuLimitExceeded` = On-Demand vCPU quota reached (request a Service Quotas increase).
expectations: Activates the aws-compute skill and distinguishes SSH `Connection timed out` (network/SG/NACL/route/changed public IP on stop-start), `Connection refused` (host reachable, `sshd` not listening/booting), and `Permission denied (publickey)` (wrong AMI default user, `chmod 400`, or 60-second EC2 Instance Connect key expiry)

Distinguishes `StatusCheckFailed_System` (AWS host hardware issue requiring a stop/start to migrate hosts, as a reboot stays on the same hardware) from `StatusCheckFailed_Instance` (guest OS/network config) and notes the opt-in ASG EBS health check

Distinguishes `InsufficientInstanceCapacity` (AWS AZ capacity shortage where a Service Quotas increase does nothing; switch AZ/type or stop/start all Cluster placement group members) from `InstanceLimitExceeded` / `VcpuLimitExceeded` (On-Demand vCPU limit requiring a Service Quotas increase)

evals.prompt: We are designing a low-latency trading and Kafka cluster on EC2 in ap-south-1. Compare the 3 EC2 Placement Group strategies (including the exact hard per-AZ limits for Spread and Partition groups and how to launch Cluster placement groups), explain what happens to data on local NVMe Instance Store volumes (`i4i` / `c7gd`) during a reboot vs stop vs host failure, and explain how public IPv4 / Elastic IP billing works.
evals.expected_output: Activates the aws-compute skill, compares the 3 Placement Group strategies: `Cluster` (packed in 1 AZ for low latency — launch all instances of the same type in a single request, and stop/start all group members on `InsufficientInstanceCapacity`), `Spread` (distinct racks with a **firm hard limit of 7 running instances per AZ per group**), and `Partition` (isolated racks per partition with a **firm hard limit of 7 partitions per AZ**); explains that **Instance Store volumes survive only a reboot** and all data is permanently lost on stop, hibernate, terminate, instance-type resize, or underlying host failure (so never store durable state or cryptographic keys/secrets on instance store); and explains that **all public IPv4 addresses are billed hourly**, including idle/unattached Elastic IPs and EIPs on stopped instances (`aws ec2 release-address`), with per-Region quota code `L-0263D0A3`.
expectations: Activates the aws-compute skill and compares `Cluster` (single AZ, launch all same-type instances in one request), `Spread` (hard limit of max 7 running instances per AZ per group), and `Partition` (hard limit of max 7 partitions per AZ) placement groups
Explains that local NVMe Instance Store data survives only an OS reboot and is permanently wiped on stop, hibernate, terminate, instance-type change, or host failure
States that all public IPv4 addresses (including idle/unattached Elastic IPs and EIPs attached to stopped instances) incur hourly charges until released (`release-address`, quota code `L-0263D0A3`)
